1:
The psalm carries the barest of headings, and the voices make what they can of it. Keil and Delitzsch observe that this is the only psalm inscribed with the single word psalm and nothing further, for which a rabbinic tractate calls it the orphan psalm; an old version heads it as concerning the redemption of the people out of Egypt, but they answer that the new song is not the song of Moses so much as its counterpart, since what resounded for the first time at the sea is here sung as a completion. They add that the opening and close are borrowed from an earlier psalm while almost everything between comes from the later chapters of Isaiah, a book of consolation that has become as it were a spring for religious song. Adam Clarke collects the titles that the versions give it, a psalm in the Hebrew, a prophetic psalm in one, a psalm of David in three others, and in another an ascription to David with a note referring it to the restoration from Egypt but bidding it be understood spiritually of the advent of the Messiah and the calling of the Gentiles. His own guess is that it was written for the deliverance from the Babylonish captivity and is to be read prophetically of the redemption of the world. John Calvin begins from its resemblance to an earlier psalm in matter and in language alike.

What makes the song new is answered differently by each. Augustine of Hippo makes it a matter of who is singing: the new man knows this song and the old man does not, the old life being derived from Adam and the new formed in Christ; and since the whole earth is commanded to sing it, those who cut themselves off from the communion of the whole earth cannot sing it at all, for it is sung in the whole and not in a part. Matthew Henry makes it new by its subject, a song of praise for redeeming love such as had not been sung before, and observes that converts change their wonder and change their joy and therefore change their note, so that grace which puts a new heart in the breast will put a new song in the mouth; in the new Jerusalem, he adds, the songs will be new to eternity and never wax old. C.H. Spurgeon dates the newness precisely: there was a new song before because the Lord was coming, and there is another now because he has come and seen and conquered. John Gill keeps it short, an excellent song for the redemption wrought and the new and living way opened.

On the right hand and the holy arm the readings converge. Augustine takes the arm for a person rather than a figure, the holy arm and the right hand being the Lord himself. Calvin presses the manner of the deliverance: the praise called for is extraordinary and not common because the salvation was singular and incredible, wrought without human means, and he notes that ordinary means, while they take nothing from the glory of God, keep us from discovering his presence so fully. Henry has the victory won by his own power against every difficulty and every enemy that stood in the way, and won not for himself only but for us. Spurgeon finds the wonder in the inadequacy of the means, since idols have fallen and superstitions withered and systems of error fled before no physical but a moral power, the energy of goodness and justice and truth. Clarke turns to the Hebrew and reports that the clause translated as victory says literally that he has made salvation for himself, as the word for marvellous things means miracles; Charles Ellicott notes in one line that the word rendered victory is more commonly rendered salvation.
2:
Salvation made known before the nations is taken as the reason for the song. John Gill distinguishes the salvation wrought from the salvation published: it was appointed, undertaken and effected, and yet remained unknown to men, and especially to the Gentile world which had no prophecy or promise of the Messiah, until it was made known in the everlasting Gospel; besides which a spirit of revelation is given to some, so that they learn their need of it and their own interest in it, and these have the new song put into their mouths. John Wesley says the same of the secret, that the redemption of the world was hitherto reserved and was not thoroughly known even by most of the people who kept the promise, and he takes the righteousness of the verse for the faithfulness that accomplished it. Adam Clarke puts the emphasis on the manner: the deliverance was so wrought as to show that it was supernatural, and that a confidence placed in the unseen God had not been in vain; the mercy remembered is the gracious promise made to the forefathers and the truth is the keeping of it.

Then the psalm turns to noise, and the expositors divide over how much of it to keep. Keil and Delitzsch read the summons as a call for some joyful manifestation of the mouth, which may be done in many ways, and find the successive verses adding first the union of song with stringed instruments, as of the Levites, and then the sound of wind instruments, as of the priests; they note that the language throughout is an echo of earlier psalms and prophets. Matthew Henry takes the whole as a coronation: the King is to be welcomed to the throne as new kings are, with acclamations and loud shouts till the earth ring again, as when Solomon was proclaimed, and since it is a victorious King the soft melody of the harp is not enough but the martial sound of trumpet and cornet must be added. He guards it at once, that carnal mirth is an enemy to this holy joy, and recalls that when David danced before the ark he pleaded that it was before the Lord. C.H. Spurgeon presses harder still, that every tongue must applaud with the vigour which joy of heart alone can arouse, and he borrows a direction from Wesley to sing lustily and with good courage and to beware of singing as if one were half dead or half asleep; yet he adds that the song must come from the heart, since otherwise the music is nothing but a noise in the ears of God, whether it be made by human throats or by organ pipes or by far-resounding trumpets.

Gill will not have the instruments at all. He reads them as an allusion to the older worship and denies that this is to be done now, holding that the newer worship is here expressed in the older language, so that when the saints are said elsewhere to have harps in their hands nothing is meant but the spiritual melody in their hearts. The smaller notes on the same verses are textual. Charles Ellicott would render the first summons as a breaking out into songs and music, and the second as playing to the Lord on a harp with melodious sound. Clarke doubts that the word translated psalm means a psalm at all, taking it either for a musical instrument or for a species of ode modulated by different voices.
6:
The instruments named in the sixth verse are chiefly a matter for the lexicon. Adam Clarke admits ignorance of the first, some kind of tubular instrument of whose form and management we know nothing, and identifies the second as the word commonly used for what we call a trumpet. Charles Ellicott adds that this is the only place in the psalm where the straight trumpet appears. John Gill begins to report how three old versions render the phrase and his note breaks off before he says what they make of it.

With the sea and the floods and the hills the question becomes whether the psalm is describing nature or people, and the voices divide cleanly. Clarke takes the roaring sea for fine poetic imagery, or, if the verse looks to the spread of the Gospel, for all maritime countries and commercial nations; he reads the rivers of the next verse as immense continents where only large rivers are found, so that inland peoples are included as well as the coasts, which in early times were nearly all that was known, and he makes the joyful hills the inhabitants of rocky and mountainous countries. Gill calls the clapping of the floods a prosopopoeia and reports a rabbinic interpreter who took the sea for those who are in ships, the rivers for the men who are in them, and the hills for those who dwell upon them. C.H. Spurgeon will have none of this reduction. The sea is the Lord’s and should not be denied a place in the orchestra of nature; its thunders are not too grand for such a theme, a great composer of choruses would have been glad of its aid, and its deep bass will excellently suit the mystery of the divine glory. He goes further and sets sacred song above the classical: the muses of Parnassus cannot rival the muse of Zion, and the Castalian fount never sparkled like that fount of every blessing to which sacred poets ascribe their inspiration.

Keil and Delitzsch keep to the figure and observe that the clapping rivers are original to this psalm, the rivers casting up high waves which flow into one another as hands are struck together. Ellicott hears in the same expression the lapping sound of waves and notes that it occurs in one of the prophets as well. Both he and Spurgeon reach for the same lines of verse to carry the mountains, four lines about the live thunder leaping from peak to peak among the rattling crags until every mountain has found a tongue; Ellicott names the poet and gives the poem, while Spurgeon quotes without naming him. Ellicott has a second poet a verse earlier, on the mighty Being awake who makes a sound like thunder everlastingly with his eternal motion.

The last verse produces Clarke’s longest note in the psalm, and it is a comparison rather than a comment. Following a bishop whose parallels he borrows, he sets this psalm beside the song of the mother of the Lord and prints five pairs in two columns, calling David the Voice and Mary the Echo: the new song answers to the soul that magnifies the Lord, the marvellous things to the great things done by him that is mighty, the right hand and holy arm to the strength shown with his arm, the salvation openly made known to the mercy on them that fear him, and the mercy and truth remembered to Israel to the help given his servant in remembrance of his mercy. He concludes that she seems to have had this psalm in her eye, and that this is a further argument that the whole of it, whatever deliverance it may record, is ultimately to be understood of the redemption of the world, for which no language is too strong and no poetic imagery too high.
